title: Prices that cannot go negative
objectives: Model a price with the lognormal distribution.
Find lognormal probabilities by taking logs and standardising.

screens.title: Double or halve
screens.prose: A £100 share will either double or halve over the year, each with chance $\tfrac12$. In logs the two moves are $+\ln 2$ and $-\ln 2$: symmetric, averaging 0.
screens.question: What is the expected price in a year?

hints.text: Average the two prices, not the two moves.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each price by its chance and add.

byKey.logs: You averaged the log moves, which cancel. The prices themselves average to more than £100.
byKey.drop: You averaged the gain and the loss as $+100$ and $-50$, then took off 50. Average the prices: $\tfrac12(200 + 50)$.

explain.text: $\tfrac12 \times 200 + \tfrac12 \times 50 = 125$. The log moves cancel, so the middle of the log outcomes is still £100. Yet the average price is higher: symmetric in logs means skewed in prices.

screens.title: Normal in logs
screens.prose: Now let the log of a price be normal: $\ln S \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ with $\mu = \ln 100$. The curve is the density of $S$ itself. Slide $\sigma$, the spread of $\ln S$.
screens.question: What happens as $\sigma$ grows?

options.text: The median stays at £100 and the mean rises above it
The median and the mean both stay at £100
options.why: Watch the mean line: it moves right as $\sigma$ grows.
The right tail stretches out. Prices can rise without limit but cannot fall below 0.

options.text: The mean falls below the median
options.why: The long right tail pulls the mean up, not down.

hints.text: Try $\sigma = 0.1$, then $\sigma = 0.8$. Watch the two lines.
The median reads £100 throughout; the mean grows.

feedback.correct: The median stays at £100; the mean climbs with $\sigma$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the caption at a small and a large $\sigma$.

explain.text: The median stays at $e^{\mu} = 100$ for every $\sigma$. The curve is squashed against 0 and stretched to the right, so the mean rises: at $\sigma = 0.8$ it is £137.71. The log of a price is the natural place for a symmetric model.

screens.title: The median
screens.prose: A variable whose log is normal is **lognormal**. It is always positive. Since $\ln$ is increasing, $S \le e^{\mu}$ exactly when $\ln S \le \mu$, and that has chance $\tfrac12$.
screens.question: If $\ln S \sim N(4.7, 0.3^2)$, what is the median of $S$? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: The median of $\ln S$ is 4.7. Undo the log.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Exponentiate the median of $\ln S$.

byKey.log: 4.7 is the median of $\ln S$. The median of $S$ is $e^{4.7}$.
byKey.mean: 115.01 is the mean, $e^{4.7 + 0.045}$. The median has no $\sigma$ in it.

explain.text: Half of $\ln S$ lies below 4.7, so half of $S$ lies below $e^{4.7} \approx 109.95$. The median passes straight through the exponential. The mean does not, as we show next.

screens.title: The mean of $e^{\sigma Z}$
screens.prose: Write $S = e^{\mu + \sigma Z}$ with $Z \sim N(0, 1)$. Then $E[S] = e^{\mu}\,E[e^{\sigma Z}]$. Find $E[e^{\sigma Z}]$ by completing the square.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $E[e^{\sigma Z}] = \displaystyle\int e^{\sigma z}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}\,dz$, the expectation of a function of $Z$
$= e^{\sigma^2/2}$, since the integral is the area under the $N(\sigma, 1)$ density, which is 1

hints.text: Merge the two exponentials before completing the square.
Definition, combine, complete the square, total area 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the integral first, and use “area 1” last.

byKey.square: Completing the square needs a single exponent, so combine first.
byKey.one: The area-1 step needs the shifted normal density in front of you.
byKey.comb: Combining needs the integral written out first.

explain.text: The leftover $\sigma^2$ from completing the square comes out as $e^{\sigma^2/2}$, and the rest is a shifted normal with area 1. So $E[S] = e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}$, above the median $e^{\mu}$ whenever $\sigma > 0$. The convexity of $e^x$ is the reason: big rises outweigh equal falls in logs.

screens.title: The mean
screens.prose: Back to $\ln S \sim N(4.7, 0.3^2)$, median £109.95. Now use $E[S] = e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}$.
screens.question: What is $E[S]$? Give 2 decimal places.

byKey.median: That is the median, $e^{4.7}$. The mean adds $\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}$ in the exponent.
byKey.full-var: You added all of $\sigma^2 = 0.09$. Add half of it.

explain.text: $e^{4.745} \approx 115.01$, about 4.6% above the median. Check: $e^{4.7} \times e^{0.045} = 109.95 \times 1.046 = 115.01$.

screens.title: A price model
screens.prose: A standard model: $$S_T = S_0\,e^{(m - \sigma^2/2)T + \sigma\sqrt{T}\,Z}.$$ The $-\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}$ cancels the $e^{\sigma^2 T/2}$ just found, so $E[S_T] = S_0e^{mT}$ for any $\sigma$. It is the volatility drag from *Series and Approximation*. Here $S_0 = 100$, $m = 0.05$, $T = 1$.
screens.question: Slide $\sigma$ towards 0. Where does all the probability end up?

options.why: The drift still acts when $\sigma = 0$: the price grows at 5% a year.
The median is $100e^{0.05 - \sigma^2/2}$, which keeps moving as $\sigma$ shrinks. It tends to 105.13.
A smaller $\sigma$ means less spread. The curve gets narrower and taller.

hints.text: Set $\sigma = 0.02$ and look at the curve and the two lines.
The median line slides towards the mean line.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $\sigma = 0$ into the model.

explain.text: At $\sigma = 0$ the model has no randomness: $S_1 = 100e^{0.05} \approx 105.13$. The density collapses to a spike there, a point mass, and the median meets the mean. Every $\sigma > 0$ pulls the median below the mean.

screens.title: Expected up, but a coin flip
screens.prose: A volatile share: $S_0 = \text{£}50$, drift $m = 8\%$ a year, volatility $\sigma = 40\%$. Its expected price in a year is $50e^{0.08} = \text{£}54.16$, so it is expected to rise 8%.
screens.question: What is $P(S_1 > 50)$, the chance it ends the year up?

options.why: You used $m = 0.08$ as the drift of $\ln S$. The log drifts at $m - \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2} = 0.08 - 0.08 = 0$.
You put a normal curve on $S$ itself, with mean 54.16. $S$ is lognormal: take logs before standardising.

options.text: More than 0.6, since it is expected to rise 8%
options.why: A high mean does not make a rise likely. A few large gains carry the mean.

hints.text: The log drift is 0, so $P(S_1 > 50) = P(Z > 0)$.

feedback.correct: The log drift is $0.08 - 0.08 = 0$, so the chance is exactly $\tfrac12$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the drift of $\ln S$, including the $-\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}$.

byKey.drift: You used $m$ without the $-\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}$. The log of the price drifts at $0.08 - 0.08 = 0$.
byKey.normal: You put a normal curve on $S$ itself. $S$ is lognormal: standardise $\ln S$, not $S$.

explain.text: The log drift is $m - \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2} = 0$, so the median price is £50 and a rise is a coin flip. The mean is still £54.16, carried by the long right tail. Expected return and the chance of a gain are different questions.

screens.title: Take logs, then standardise
screens.prose: For $S_T = S_0\,e^{(m - \sigma^2/2)T + \sigma\sqrt T Z}$: $$P(S_T > K) = 1 - \Phi\left(\frac{\ln(K/S_0) - (m - \tfrac12\sigma^2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}\right).$$ The median is $S_0e^{(m - \sigma^2/2)T}$ and the mean is $S_0e^{mT}$.
screens.question: With $m = 0$ and $\sigma > 0$, how does $P(S_T > S_0)$ compare with $\tfrac12$?

options.why: That needs the log drift $m - \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}$ to be 0. With $m = 0$ it is $-\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2} < 0$.
With $m = 0$ the log drifts down, at $-\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}$, so the median falls below $S_0$.

hints.text: Put $K = S_0$ and $m = 0$ into the formula.
$\ln(K/S_0) = 0$, so the fraction is $\tfrac{\sigma^2 T/2}{\sigma\sqrt T} = \tfrac{\sigma\sqrt T}{2}$.
$1 - \Phi$ of a positive number is below $\tfrac12$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Substitute $K = S_0$ and $m = 0$ and check the sign of the $z$.

explain.text: The $z$ is $\tfrac{\sigma\sqrt T}{2} > 0$, so $P(S_T > S_0) = 1 - \Phi\left(\tfrac{\sigma\sqrt T}{2}\right) < \tfrac12$. A share with zero expected return falls more often than it rises. Its mean holds up through rare large gains.

screens.title: Will it reach £120?
screens.prose: A £100 share has drift $m = 5\%$ and volatility $\sigma = 20\%$ a year. A trader holds a digital option that pays if the share ends the year above £120.
screens.question: What is $P(S_1 > 120)$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Standardise $\ln(120/100)$ with log drift $0.05 - 0.02$ and sd 0.2.

byKey.normal: You put a normal on $S_1$ with its mean and sd. $S_1$ is lognormal: standardise $\ln S_1$.
byKey.no-drag: You used $m = 0.05$ as the log drift. Subtract $\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2} = 0.02$ first.
byKey.simple: You used the simple return 0.2 in place of $\ln 1.2 \approx 0.1823$.
byKey.no-drift: You left out the drift. The log drifts up by $0.05 - 0.02 = 0.03$ in the year.

explain.text: $\ln 1.2 \approx 0.1823$, so $z = \tfrac{0.1823 - 0.03}{0.2} \approx 0.7616$ and the option pays with chance 0.2231. The median price is $100e^{0.03} \approx \text{£}103.05$ and the mean is $100e^{0.05} \approx \text{£}105.13$.

screens.title: Below its own average
screens.prose: Same share: median price in a year £103.05, mean £105.13. A client asks how often the share ends the year below its expected price.
screens.question: What is $P(S_1 < 105.13)$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Standardise $\ln(105.13/100)$ as before.

byKey.half: 0.5 is the chance of ending below the median, £103.05. The mean sits higher.
byKey.above: 0.4602 is the chance of ending above the mean.

explain.text: $\ln(105.13/100) = 0.05$, so $z = \tfrac{0.05 - 0.03}{0.2} = 0.1$ and $\Phi(0.1) \approx 0.54$. In general $z = \tfrac{\sigma\sqrt T}{2}$: more volatility, more years below the average. A few large gains carry the mean.

ideas: If $\ln S \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ then $S$ is lognormal: positive and right-skewed, with median $e^{\mu}$ and mean $e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}$.
$E[e^{\sigma Z}] = e^{\sigma^2/2}$, so the price model $S_T = S_0e^{(m - \sigma^2/2)T + \sigma\sqrt T Z}$ has $E[S_T] = S_0e^{mT}$. The $-\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}$ is the volatility drag.
For a probability, take logs and standardise: $P(S_T > K) = 1 - \Phi\left(\tfrac{\ln(K/S_0) - (m - \sigma^2/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt T}\right)$.

formula.name: Lognormal median and mean
formula.note: The mean exceeds the median whenever $\sigma > 0$.

summary.trap: Do not put a normal curve on $S$, and do not use $m$ as the drift of $\ln S$: the log drifts at $m - \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}$.

byKey.full-var: You added all of $\sigma^2$. Add half: 0.125.

quiz.prose: A share has $S_0 = 100$, $m = 0$ and $\sigma = 25\%$ a year.
quiz.question: What is $P(S_4 > 100)$, the chance it is up after 4 years? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The log drifts at $-\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}$ a year, and the log sd is $\sigma\sqrt T$.

byKey.half: With $m = 0$ the log still drifts down at $\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}$ a year, so the median falls below 100.
byKey.flip: 0.5987 is the chance it is down.

explain.text: $\ln(S_4/100) \sim N(-0.125, 0.5^2)$, so $z = \tfrac{0 + 0.125}{0.5} = 0.25$ and the chance is $1 - \Phi(0.25) \approx 0.4013$. Zero expected return, yet down 6 times in 10.

$e^{\mu}$ is the median. The mean is $e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}$.
